title: Finite Projective Plane of Order q
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A projective plane of order q has q^2+q+1 points and lines, each line contains q+1 points, and any two points lie on a unique line.
short: It is the incidence geometry of one-dimensional subspaces of F_q^3.
long: It is the incidence geometry of one-dimensional subspaces of F_q^3. Points and lines are the one- and two-dimensional subspaces of a three-dimensional vector space.
proof: Count subspaces and use dimension-two intersections to verify the axioms.
consequence: Projective planes supply symmetric designs and finite geometries.

title: Incidence Matrix Identity of a Projective Plane
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For a projective plane of order q with incidence matrix A, the product A times A transpose equals qI+J.
short: Two points lie together on exactly one line.
long: Two points lie together on exactly one line. The diagonal entries count q+1 lines through a point, while off-diagonal entries count one common line.
proof: The (i,j) entry counts lines containing both points i and j.
consequence: It gives an immediate spectral description of projective planes.

title: Parameter Equations for Balanced Incomplete Designs
subject: Combinatorics
statement: In a 2-(v,k,lambda) design, the replication number r and block count b satisfy vr=lambda(v-1) and bk=vr.
short: Count point-block incidences in two ways.
long: Count point-block incidences in two ways. Counting pairs containing a fixed point gives the first equation; counting all incidences gives the second.
proof: Double-count incidences and pairs of points lying in blocks.
consequence: These equations constrain all feasible design parameters.

title: Small Ramsey Number R(3,4)
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Ramsey number R(3,4) equals 9: every red-blue colouring of K_9 has a red triangle or a blue K_4, and K_8 has a colouring avoiding both.
short: Nine vertices force a triangle or a four-clique.
long: Nine vertices force a triangle or a four-clique. The lower bound uses an explicit 8-vertex colouring based on the cube.
proof: Upper bound follows from degree counting; lower bound is exhibited by a concrete colouring.
consequence: It is a classic exactly known off-diagonal Ramsey number.

title: Diagonal Ramsey Number R(4,4)
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Ramsey number R(4,4) equals 18.
short: Eighteen vertices force a monochromatic four-clique.
long: Eighteen vertices force a monochromatic four-clique. The lower bound comes from a 17-vertex colouring; the upper bound used extensive case analysis and computation.
proof: Greenwood and Gleason gave the lower construction and an exhaustive argument for the upper bound.
consequence: It is one of the few exactly known diagonal Ramsey numbers.

title: Van der Waerden's Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every finite colouring of the positive integers contains monochromatic arithmetic progressions of every length.
short: Any finite colouring forces long regular patterns.
long: Any finite colouring forces long regular patterns. The proof uses induction on progression length and a notion of coloured arithmetic progressions of progressions.
proof: The original double-induction argument builds longer progressions from many shorter aligned ones.
consequence: It is a foundational result of Ramsey theory on the integers.

title: Schur's Theorem on Sum-Free Colour Classes
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every finite colouring of the positive integers yields a monochromatic triple x,y,z with x+y=z.
short: No finite colouring can make every colour class sum-free.
long: No finite colouring can make every colour class sum-free. It follows from Ramsey's theorem applied to differences, or from finite Schur numbers.
proof: Colour edges of a complete graph on (N+1) vertices by the colour of their difference.
consequence: It connects colouring to additive structure.

title: Rado's Criterion for Partition Regular Equations
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A homogeneous linear equation is partition regular over the positive integers if and only if some nonempty subset of its coefficients sums to zero.
short: A zero coefficient sum is exactly what is needed.
long: A zero coefficient sum is exactly what is needed. The criterion extends to systems via the columns condition.
proof: Necessity uses a colouring by powers of a prime; sufficiency uses the partition condition in a Rado matrix.
consequence: It classifies which linear equations survive every finite colouring.

title: Hales-Jewett Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For every alphabet size k and colour count r there is N such that every r-colouring of the Hamming cube [k]^N contains a monochromatic combinatorial line.
short: High-dimensional words force a variable-word pattern.
long: High-dimensional words force a variable-word pattern. A combinatorial line fixes some coordinates and lets the others vary together.
proof: The original proof uses induction on the alphabet and colour count with a density increment.
consequence: It implies van der Waerden's theorem and underlies density Ramsey theory.

title: Density Hales-Jewett Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every subset of [k]^N of positive density contains a combinatorial line when N is large enough.
short: Positive density is enough to force a line.
long: Positive density is enough to force a line. It is the density analogue of Hales-Jewett and implies Szemeredi's theorem.
proof: Polymath1 gave a proof using hypergraph regularity and density increment.
consequence: It unifies density and Ramsey results on words and integers.

title: Erdos-Szekeres Monotone Subsequence Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Any sequence of (r-1)(s-1)+1 distinct real numbers has an increasing subsequence of length r or a decreasing subsequence of length s.
short: Long sequences force long monotone patterns.
long: Long sequences force long monotone patterns. The bound is sharp by a standard block construction.
proof: Assign to each entry the lengths of the best increasing and decreasing subsequences ending there and use pigeonhole.
consequence: It is a classical intersection of combinatorics and analysis.

title: Mirsky's Theorem on Chain Partitions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: In a finite poset, the minimum number of antichains needed to cover the poset equals the size of a largest chain.
short: Dual to Dilworth's theorem, chains and antichains exchange roles.
long: Dual to Dilworth's theorem, chains and antichains exchange roles. Ranking each element by the longest chain ending at it gives the optimal antichain layers.
proof: The layers are antichains, and every chain meets each layer at most once.
consequence: It provides a constructive decomposition of finite posets.

title: LYM Inequality for Antichains
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For an antichain in the Boolean lattice on n elements, the sum over its members of 1 over C(n,size) is at most 1.
short: A random maximal chain meets an antichain at most once.
long: A random maximal chain meets an antichain at most once. It implies Sperner's theorem because the smallest coefficient is 1 over C(n,floor(n/2)).
proof: Choose a random permutation and count the probability that its maximal chain passes through each member.
consequence: It gives a probabilistic proof of the Sperner bound.

title: Kruskal-Katona Shadow Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Among k-uniform families of a fixed size, the initial segment in colexicographic order has the smallest possible lower shadow.
short: Packing sets as early as possible minimizes their shadows.
long: Packing sets as early as possible minimizes their shadows. The lower shadow consists of all (k-1)-subsets of members of the family.
proof: Repeated compressions move any family to a colex initial segment without increasing the shadow.
consequence: It controls face numbers of simplicial complexes.

title: Bollobas's Two Families Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: If A_i and B_i satisfy A_i intersect B_i empty and A_i intersect B_j nonempty whenever i<j, then the sum of 1 over C(|A_i|+|B_i|,|A_i|) is at most 1.
short: Cross-intersecting pairs cannot be too numerous.
long: Cross-intersecting pairs cannot be too numerous. It generalizes results about skew Bollobas systems and set-pair inequalities.
proof: Consider random permutations of each union and show the relevant orderings are disjoint.
consequence: It is a standard tool for extremal set theory.

title: Turan's Theorem on Forbidden Complete Subgraphs
subject: Combinatorics
statement: An n-vertex graph with no clique of size r+1 has at most (1-1/r)n^2/2 edges, with equality for the balanced complete r-partite graph.
short: Balanced complete multipartite graphs are extremal.
long: Balanced complete multipartite graphs are extremal. The exact extremal graph is the Turan graph T_r(n).
proof: Zykov symmetrization turns any extremal graph into a complete multipartite one, then balancing parts maximizes edges.
consequence: It begins extremal graph theory and quantifies clique avoidance.

title: Mantel's Triangle-Free Edge Bound
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A triangle-free graph on n vertices has at most floor(n^2/4) edges.
short: The complete bipartite graph is the best triangle-free choice.
long: The complete bipartite graph is the best triangle-free choice. It is the case r=2 of Turan's theorem.
proof: For each edge uv, degrees d(u)+d(v)<=n; summing over edges and applying Cauchy-Schwarz gives the bound.
consequence: It is the oldest extremal graph theorem.

title: Kovari-Sos-Turan Bound for Bipartite Forbidden Graphs
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For s at most t, the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph with no K_{s,t} is at most O(n^{2-1/s}).
short: Counting common neighbours bounds bipartite subgraph density.
long: Counting common neighbours bounds bipartite subgraph density. The order is correct when t is large enough relative to s.
proof: Double-count pairs consisting of an s-set of vertices and a common neighbour, using convexity.
consequence: It covers extremal problems that Turan's theorem cannot resolve.

title: Szemeredi Regularity Lemma
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every large graph admits a partition into a bounded number of parts such that almost every pair of parts behaves pseudorandomly.
latex: \forall\varepsilon\;\exists M:\text{}\varepsilon\text{-regular partition with at most }M\text{ parts}
short: Large graphs can be approximated by weighted random-looking graphs.
long: Large graphs can be approximated by weighted random-looking graphs. A pair is epsilon-regular if edge densities between all sufficiently large subparts are close.
proof: Refine partitions whenever irregular pairs remain; a mean-square density potential strictly increases.
consequence: It underlies the graph removal lemma and property testing.

title: Graph Removal Lemma
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For every fixed graph H and tolerance epsilon, a graph with few copies of H can be made H-free by deleting at most epsilon n^2 edges.
short: Few forbidden subgraphs can be destroyed cheaply.
long: Few forbidden subgraphs can be destroyed cheaply. It follows from the regularity lemma and the counting lemma.
proof: Regularize the graph, remove edges inside parts and between irregular or forbidden-density pairs.
consequence: It gives deletion versions of many extremal results and underlies property testing.

title: Graham-Pollak Biclique Partition Bound
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Partitioning the edge set of the complete graph on n vertices into complete bipartite subgraphs requires at least n-1 subgraphs.
short: Linear algebra forces many bicliques.
long: Linear algebra forces many bicliques. The decomposition into stars shows n-1 is attainable.
proof: Assign a real variable to each vertex and use the linear independence of the corresponding rank-one matrices.
consequence: It is a classic algebraic lower bound in combinatorics.

title: Rank Sizes of the Boolean Lattice
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of k-element subsets of an n-element set is C(n,k), so the rank sizes of the Boolean lattice are binomial coefficients.
short: The k-th layer consists of all k-subsets.
long: The k-th layer consists of all k-subsets. The total number of elements in the Boolean lattice is 2^n.
proof: By definition, a k-subset is chosen by selecting k of n elements.
consequence: It makes the Boolean lattice the basic example of a graded poset.

title: Mobius Function of the Boolean Lattice
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For subsets S contained in T, the poset Mobius function equals (-1) to the size of T minus S.
short: Alternating signs cancel over intermediate subsets.
long: Alternating signs cancel over intermediate subsets. It is the poset analogue of the classical number-theoretic Mobius inversion.
proof: The defining recurrence sums (-1)^j C(|T|-|S|,j), which is zero unless S=T.
consequence: It yields inclusion-exclusion as a special case of poset inversion.

title: Incidence Algebra and Zeta Inversion
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The incidence algebra of a locally finite poset has convolution as product, and the inverse of the zeta function is the Mobius function.
short: Poset inversion generalizes summation by parts.
long: Poset inversion generalizes summation by parts. The zeta function is 1 on every comparable pair and its convolution inverse is mu.
proof: The recursive definition of mu is exactly the equation zeta * mu = delta.
consequence: It unifies many inversion formulas on partially ordered sets.

title: Every Finite Nonempty Poset Has a Minimal Element
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every nonempty finite partially ordered set contains at least one minimal element.
short: Following a descending chain must stop.
long: Following a descending chain must stop. There may be several minimal elements, and they need not be comparable.
proof: Start anywhere and move to a smaller element until no smaller element exists; finiteness forces termination.
consequence: It underlies greedy algorithms and inductive arguments on posets.
